title: Hitchhiking Across America with David Choe (Full Documentary)
summary: David Choe and Harry Kim cross the United States without paying for rides, moving by freight train, hitchhiking, casino hospitality, an inflatable river tube, private vehicles and a farm-worker bus. The film documents generosity, precarity, addiction, danger, post-Katrina testimony, racial and sexual stereotyping, exploitation of incidental participants and Choe's simultaneous attraction to and revulsion toward America. Every idea remains; observation, narration, interview testimony, joke, stereotype, uncertain edit and independently verifiable fact stay distinct.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological human read and full-source correction/context pass. The automatic captions are useful but heavily damage places, names, songs and closing lyrics. A matching VICE manual-caption source now overrides the opening 1,192.29 seconds at the text-evidence layer and supplies publisher labels; those labels are not claimed as acoustic-model output.

speaker_policy: David Choe and Harry Kim are public principals and some incidental people introduce themselves on camera, but visual presence does not prove every line. Publish no line-level names until held-out acoustic/video validation; do not identity-resolve incidental participants from travel, family, legal or location clues.

connections.relationship: The no-paid-rides rule turns travel dependence into the documentary's social engine.
Choe opens danger as comedy while also disclosing prior assault and a contested survivor theory.
Theft, Christian conversion and gambling appear as successive ways of organizing desire.
Casino hospitality and credit create movement while repeatedly threatening the journey itself.
Anger at drivers' evasions ends in Choe recognizing that he would share their reluctance.
Travelers describe strangers' generosity as the infrastructure of low-money movement.
A traveler's route follows survivable weather rather than romantic adventure.
Mobile freedom is voiced beside survival, waiting, poverty and dependence.
The vehicle becomes a short-lived shelter for people, dogs and conflicting life stories.
Visible hate symbols prompt Choe to invent creators and gender dynamics that the wall cannot prove.
Off-camera prejudice is preserved as Choe's report rather than generalized to a restaurant or city.
A credit advance and blackjack win bankroll an unsafe river plan.
Repeated local cautions become part of the film's drama rather than changing the conduct.
Bodily exposure and visible discharge complicate the romantic river image.
The choice to continue after dark pairs Choe's strongest joy with escalating physical risk.
A romantic river arrival becomes dependence on armed private-property owners.
A perceived noose beside cotton produces historically grounded fear but still requires visual verification.
The travelogue shifts from adventure to visible devastation and resident testimony.
A resident returns despite death, isolation and poor habitability because home and family remain there.
A host resident answers the film's racial anxiety with a concrete family rule about conduct rather than color.
The travelers' chosen drift meets a participant whose movement and wages are controlled by work release.
The incarcerated participant rejects Choe's escape fantasy; that refusal is the authoritative event.
A possible ride-for-work exchange raises translation, wage and documentary-power questions.
Choe's final love letter uses graphic incest, violence and rape metaphors before arriving at affection and forgiveness.

source_notes.claim: The full documentary's automatic captions are the best available text for its opening.
source_notes.assessment: VICE manual-caption source QO3-AAVTeDA matches the complete opening sequence through 1192.29 seconds and is the accepted text overlay there. It materially repairs slurs, names, places and claim meaning while preserving [INAUDIBLE].

source_notes.claim: The quoted rail-yard fines and jail rule are current law.
source_notes.assessment: They are an incidental speaker's historical account; verify railroad, jurisdiction and date, and never use them for evasion guidance.

source_notes.claim: Choe's theft, conversion and gambling chronology is independently proven.
source_notes.assessment: The film provides first-person narration edited for a travel documentary; preserve it as self-report.

source_notes.claim: The film's sentence fully describes Chinese and Black railroad labor.
source_notes.assessment: It points toward real labor history but needs railroad-specific primary history, dates, regions and distinct worker experiences.

source_notes.claim: The incidental musician took two lessons from Jerry Garcia.
source_notes.assessment: This is first-person oral history and needs corroboration before entering a public-figure timeline.

source_notes.claim: Children in Moriarty begin drinking at six.
source_notes.assessment: A local participant's likely hyperbole is not town-level public-health evidence.

source_notes.claim: An Amarillo restaurant or its workers hold the reported anti-Black view.
source_notes.assessment: Choe recounts off-camera comments by unidentified waitresses after they declined filming; do not attribute the claim to a venue, city or workforce.

source_notes.claim: The Mississippi contains the exact hazards described as sinkholes.
source_notes.assessment: Local speakers repeatedly warn of current, barges and deaths, but terminology and comparative-danger claims need authoritative river-safety sources.

source_notes.claim: Everyone locals knew who swam in the Mississippi died.
source_notes.assessment: This is Choe's compressed/exaggerated summary, not mortality data.

source_notes.claim: The tube traveled the stated miles and could reach the stated destination on schedule.
source_notes.assessment: Distances, speed, current and route are narration estimates, not navigational records.

source_notes.claim: The visible object was a racist noose placed to threaten travelers.
source_notes.assessment: Choe perceives a noose near a cotton field and reacts with historically grounded fear; inspect the frame and provenance before assigning intent.

source_notes.claim: The New Orleans scenes occurred exactly one year after Katrina.
source_notes.assessment: Verify filming dates, exact levee-breach site and recovery chronology against primary records.

source_notes.claim: The named family deaths and Houston circumstances are fully established.
source_notes.assessment: They are a resident's direct account but remain sensitive; public-record verification needs a real editorial purpose before indexing names.

source_notes.claim: Four DUIs automatically produce the stated felony and sentence.
source_notes.assessment: The participant describes his own case conversationally; verify offense dates, Alabama law, sentence and program separately.

source_notes.claim: The workers' employer, immigration status and free-labor terms are known.
source_notes.assessment: The edited scene and translated exchange do not establish any of those facts; verify credits and consent before further identification.
